results.summary: This project implements a small 4x4-bit memory using D flip-flops, where four data inputs are stored at an address selected by two address bits when write enable is asserted. The stored data is continuously output on four pins corresponding to the selected address. It is designed for the Wokwi simulator and requires external clock, reset, write enable, address, and data switches, with outputs readable via LEDs. The design is a basic educational memory block with no silicon test results reported.

This design uses three AND gates to drive a 7-segment display so that pressing the first four input buttons displays the letter 'M'. The outputs correspond to the seven segments plus a dot, and the inputs are four buttons. It is intended for the Wokwi simulator and serves as a simple demonstration of combinational logic. No silicon test results are provided.

This project combines four sub-designs—a shift register, a hexadecimal seven-segment encoder, a 1-bit ALU, and a 3-bit adder—selectable via two project-select pins. The remaining six inputs are used for data and control depending on the selected mode, and outputs drive a 7-segment display or provide results. It is built for the Wokwi simulator and is intended as a multi-purpose educational tool. No silicon test results are reported.

This design stores a single decimal digit (0–9) and displays it on a 7-segment display. It has clock and reset inputs and outputs for the seven segments and dot. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no explanation of how it works or how to test it. It is implemented in Wokwi and lacks any silicon test results.

This project implements a 4-bit S-box for the SKINNY cipher algorithm. It takes four input bits and produces four output bits according to the S-box mapping. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no explanation of how it works or how to test it. It is implemented in Wokwi and lacks any silicon test results.

This project implements a stateful combination lock that requires three correct codes in sequence to unlock. A two-bit state machine tracks progress, and any wrong code resets to the initial state. The lock status is output on a single pin, and inputs include reset, enter, and five code-digit pins. It is designed for the Wokwi simulator and is described as an experiment or puzzle; no silicon test results are provided.

This project implements Ascon's 5-bit S-box, a cryptographic substitution box used in the Ascon cipher. It takes five input bits and produces five output bits according to the S-box definition. The documentation references external papers for details but provides no local explanation. It is implemented in Wokwi and lacks any silicon test results.

This project implements an 8-bit S-box for the SKINNY cipher algorithm. It takes eight input bits and produces eight output bits according to the S-box mapping. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no explanation of how it works or how to test it. It is implemented in Wokwi and lacks any silicon test results.

This project implements a binary door lock that takes an 8-bit input and opens only when a specific combination is entered. With 8 bits, there are 256 possible combinations, and only one sets the output high. It is designed for the Wokwi simulator and can be tested there. No silicon test results are provided.

This project implements a whac-a-mole style game called 'Catch the fish', using a 6-bit Fibonacci LFSR and a simple timer to generate pseudo-random outputs. Players press one of three buttons when the corresponding feedback output is high to score, with a reward feedback provided. It requires a clock and three buttons, and outputs feedback signals. It is designed for the Wokwi simulator and is a game; no silicon test results are reported.
